items.followUp: State the octet rule and explain how sodium attains a stable outer shell.

rubric.why: The rule is defined by the number of electrons in the outermost shell.
rubric.description: States that the outermost (valence) shell has eight electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the eight-electron requirement in the outermost or valence shell.

rubric.why: The octet rule describes the stable arrangement atoms attain.
rubric.description: Connects the octet to the stable configuration of noble gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms attain a stable noble-gas-like configuration.

modelAnswer: The octet rule states that atoms gain, lose or share electrons to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell.
This gives them a stable electronic configuration like that of noble gases.

items.followUp: Define a coordinate covalent bond and state how it differs from an ordinary covalent bond.

rubric.why: Sharing of electrons is the defining feature of a covalent bond.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed by mutual sharing of electron pair(s).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the idea of mutual sharing of electrons between atoms.

rubric.why: The question also asks for the three types, classified by the number of shared pairs.
rubric.description: Names single, double and triple covalent bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming all three types.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms mutually share one or more pairs of electrons.
Its three types are single, double and triple covalent bonds.

items.followUp: How do stronger intermolecular forces affect the boiling point of a liquid?

rubric.why: The effect of intermolecular force strength on evaporation must be identified.
rubric.description: States the relationship between force strength and evaporation rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that stronger forces slow evaporation, or weaker forces increase it.

rubric.why: Evaporation depends on molecules escaping from the liquid surface.
rubric.description: Explains that stronger attractions make it harder for molecules to escape.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger attractions to fewer molecules escaping or a greater energy barrier.

modelAnswer: Stronger intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules more tightly, so fewer molecules can escape from the surface and evaporation is slower.
Weaker intermolecular forces allow molecules to escape more easily, so evaporation is faster.

items.followUp: What happens to the forward and reverse reaction rates when a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium?

rubric.why: Equal forward and reverse reaction rates are essential to dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explicitly stating equality of the two rates.

rubric.why: At equilibrium, equal rates mean there is no net change in amounts of reactants and products.
rubric.description: States that concentrations remain constant while both reactions continue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for constant concentrations or amounts at equilibrium, with the reaction understood to continue.

modelAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a closed system where the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.

items.followUp: Write any four physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: The question requires four physical properties; each correct distinct property contributes to the answer.
rubric.description: Gives any four physical properties of metals.
rubric.how: Award 0.5 mark for each of four distinct correct properties (2 marks total). The listed combinations are examples of acceptable sets.

modelAnswer: Metals are sonorous and generally conduct heat and electricity well.

items.followUp: What is meant by the scattering of light by a colloid?

rubric.why: The Tyndall effect is caused by scattering of light by colloidal particles.
rubric.description: Identifies scattering of light by colloidal particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the particles as the cause of light scattering.

rubric.why: Scattering makes the path of a light beam visible through a colloid.
rubric.description: States that the scattered beam or path of light becomes visible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the visible light path or beam.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light passing through a colloid.
This scattering makes the path of the beam visible; this phenomenon is called the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: Define percentage mass by mass (% m/m) and give an example.

rubric.why: The notation describes the volume of solute relative to a fixed mass of solution.
rubric.description: Defines % V/M as millilitres of solute in 100 g of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct volume-per-mass basis and the 100 g of solution denominator.

rubric.why: A numerical example demonstrates the meaning of the percentage notation.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as 5% V/M meaning 5 mL solute in 100 g solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a consistent numerical example with units.

modelAnswer: % V/M means the volume of solute, in millilitres, present in 100 g of solution.
For example, a 5% V/M solution contains 5 mL of solute in 100 g of solution.

items.followUp: Define molality and write its unit.

rubric.why: Molarity is defined using the amount of solute and volume of solution.
rubric.description: Defines molarity as moles of solute per unit volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition, preferably specifying one dm³ or one litre of solution.

rubric.why: A correct concentration unit is required in addition to the definition.
rubric.description: Gives the unit mol dm⁻³ or mol L⁻¹ (M).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct molarity unit.

modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm³ (litre) of solution.
Its unit is mol dm⁻³, also written as mol L⁻¹ or M.
